name: Noni juice (Morinda citrifolia)
short: Case reports describe acute liver injury after noni juice and high blood potassium in a man with kidney disease. A 2007 review advised vigilance but said a European food safety body saw no liver link.
text: The reports of harm are individual case reports. One describes a man with chronic kidney insufficiency who had high blood potassium while drinking noni juice despite reporting a low-potassium diet; the juice samples contained 56.3 mEq/L of potassium, similar to orange or tomato juice, and the authors warned that such products may be hidden sources of potassium for people with kidney disease. Two case reports describe acute liver injury: a 45-year-old man with highly elevated liver enzymes after drinking noni juice for three weeks, in whom there was no evidence for viral hepatitis, Epstein-Barr virus or cytomegalovirus, autoimmune hepatitis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, haemochromatosis or Wilson's disease, a liver biopsy was reported to confirm herbal toxicity and enzyme levels returned to normal within a month of stopping; and a previously healthy 14-year-old boy with acute liver toxicity after drinking noni berry juice. On the other side, a review published in 2007, before the 2011 report of the boy, states that noni juice was considered safe on the basis of a toxicological assessment, that the safety question had been re-examined in Europe because of then-recent reports of liver toxicity (the abstract does not say which reports or who re-examined it), and that the European Food Safety Authority saw no link between noni juice and adverse liver effects, although the review's authors advised continued monitoring and some vigilance. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
